claim: Acral melanoma (AM) exhibits a high incidence in Asian patients with melanoma.
source: Acral melanoma (AM) exhibits a high incidence in Asian patients with melanoma, and it is not well treated with immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of AM in Asian populations.

claim: Acral melanoma is not well treated with immunotherapy.
source: Acral melanoma (AM) exhibits a high incidence in Asian patients with melanoma, and it is not well treated with immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known limitation of current treatment approaches.

claim: Genes such as TWIST1, EREG, TNFRSF9, and CTGF could drive the deregulation of various TME components.
source: Our analysis revealed that genes, such as TWIST1, EREG, TNFRSF9, and CTGF could drive the deregulation of various TME components.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single-cell RNA sequencing analysis and computational methods described in the study.

claim: The molecular interaction relationships between TME cells, such as MIF-CD44 and TNFSF9-TNFRSF9, might be an attractive target for developing novel immunotherapeutic agents.
source: The molecular interaction relationships between TME cells, such as MIF-CD44 and TNFSF9-TNFRSF9, might be an attractive target for developing novel immunotherapeutic agents.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed molecular interactions in the study.

claim: Approximately 300,000 new cases and 60,000 deaths from malignant melanoma are recorded every year.
source: Approximately 300,000 new cases and 60,000 deaths are recorded every year.
evidence: This is stated as epidemiological data in the introduction, citing Swick and Maize, 2012.

claim: Metastatic melanoma is the most fatal type of cancer.
source: However, metastatic melanoma is the most fatal type of cancer (Wahid et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wahid et al., 2018.

claim: Patients with metastatic melanoma have a 5-year survival rate of <10%.
source: However, metastatic melanoma is the most fatal type of cancer (Wahid et al., 2018), beceuse patients are susceptible to relapse after surgery, resulting in a poor prognosis and a 5-year survival rate of <10% (McKean and Amaria, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKean and Amaria, 2018.

claim: The proportion of AM cases of the total melanomas in Asians is as high as 70%.
source: In contrast to the epidemiological data of a proportion of <10% AMs out of the total number of cases of melanoma in the European-descent populations, the proportion of AM cases of the total melanomas in Asians is as high as 70% (Chi et al., 2011; Cormier et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chi et al., 2011 and Cormier et al., 2006.

claim: Terminal AMs have been considered as a subtype of melanoma with poor prognosis and poor immune efficacy.
source: and terminal AMs have been considered as a subtype of melanoma with poor prognosis and poor immune efficacy (Nakamura et al., 2020; Rose et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2020 and Rose et al., 2021.

claim: A total of 61,726 single cells were used for downstream analyses after quality control and removal of batch effects.
source: After quality control and removal of batch effects, a total of 61,726 single cells were used for downstream analyses (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data processing results, with reference to supporting figures.

claim: Aneuploid mutant cells were identified as malignant cells, which were derived specifically from primary and LG metastatic tissues.
source: According to the copy number variation (CNV) results by CopyKAT (Gao et al., 2021), we initially identified aneuploid mutant cells as malignant cells, which were derived specifically from primary and LG metastatic tissues
evidence: This claim is based on CNV analysis using CopyKAT method, as cited.

claim: Diploid mutant cells were identified as cells of the other microenvironmental components.
source: and diploid mutant cells were identified as cells of the other microenvironmental components (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is based on CNV analysis results shown in the referenced figure.

claim: All cells were defined as malignant cells (MITF+, 21,624 cells), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs; COL1A1+, 17,434 cells), T cells (CD3D+, 8322 cells), macrophages (C1QB+, 5520 cells), endothelial cells (PECAM1+, 4033 cells), neutrophils (S100A8+, 2519 cells), B cells (CD79A+, 1007 cells), epithelial cells (EPCAM+, 657 cells), and keratinocytes (KRT14+, 607 cells).
source: All cells were defined as malignant cells (MITF+, 21,624 cells), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs; COL1A1+, 17,434 cells), T cells (CD3D+, 8322 cells), macrophages (C1QB+, 5520 cells), endothelial cells (PECAM1+, 4033 cells), neutrophils (S100A8+, 2519 cells), B cells (CD79A+, 1007 cells), epithelial cells (EPCAM+, 657 cells), and keratinocytes (KRT14+, 607 cells) (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is based on cell type annotation using marker genes and SingleR, with supporting figures.

claim: In the PLs, the AMs had a higher proportion of malignant cells and CAFs, but a lower proportion of lymphocyte infiltrations compared to non-acral skin CM.
source: In the PLs, the AMs had a higher proportion of malignant cells and CAFs, but a lower proportion of lymphocyte infiltrations (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published scRNA-seq data from non-acral skin CM, as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There was a larger proportion of CAFs in the metastatic LG of AM compared to CMs, which was almost absent in the metastatic LGs of CMs.
source: In the metastatic LGs, the proportion of malignant cells was similar between AMs and CMs, but there was still a larger proportion of CAFs in the metastatic LG of AM, which was almost absent in the metastatic LGs of CMs.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published CM data.

claim: The endothelial cells and fibroblasts in PLs of AMs interacted more closely with other types of cells compared to CMs.
source: The endothelial cells and fibroblasts in PLs of AMs interacted more closely with other types of cells, while the secretion signals of immune and myeloid cells in CMs were more active (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is based on cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The malignant cells in metastatic LG of AM secreted stronger signals to the immune and myeloid cells compared to CMs.
source: Furthermore, the malignant cells in metastatic LG of AM secreted stronger signals to the immune and myeloid cells, while other interactions were weaker (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is based on cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The communications among cells in the primary tissues were closer compared to adjacent tissues and LG metastatic tissues.
source: The results demonstrated that the communications among cells in the primary tissues were closer (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on CellChat analysis of cell-cell interactions shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: In the ATs, KIT and WNT cell interaction signaling pathways were specifically identified.
source: In the ATs, KIT and WNT cell interaction signaling pathways were specifically identified, in which KIT signals were secreted primarily by endothelial cells and fibroblasts, and WNT signals were primarily secreted by keratinocytes.
evidence: This is based on CellChat analysis of signaling pathways.

claim: In the primary tissues, NT, ncWNT, IL1, and GDF cell interaction signaling pathways were specifically identified.
source: In the primary tissues, NT, ncWNT, IL1, and GDF cell interaction signaling pathways were specifically identified. NT, ncWNT, and GDF signals were secreted primarily by malignant cells, and IL1 signals were secreted primarily by neutrophils.
evidence: This is based on CellChat analysis of signaling pathways.

claim: Chemerin, NRG, and GDF cell interaction signaling pathways were specifically identified in the LG metastatic tissues.
source: Chemerin, NRG, and GDF cell interaction signaling pathways were specifically identified in the LG metastatic tissues. Chemerin and NRG signals were mainly secreted by malignant cells, and PSAP signals were primarily secreted by macrophages (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is based on CellChat analysis of signaling pathways shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Compared to the PLs, in the LG, the outgoing and incoming interaction capabilities of malignant cells in the TMEs increased.
source: Compared to the PLs, in the LG, the outgoing and incoming interaction capabilities of malignant cells in the TMEs increased, and the interactions among malignant cells and macrophages, B and T cells and fibroblasts increased.
evidence: This is based on CellChat analysis comparing interaction strengths between PLs and LG.

claim: Cells in subcluster 3 of malignant cells were in an earlier state, whereas cells in subcluster 1 were in a more terminal state.
source: The pseudotime analyses inferred from splicing kinetics showed that cells in subcluster 3 were in an earlier state, whereas cells in subcluster 1 were in a more terminal state (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity and pseudotime analysis shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Transcription factor TWIST1 was highly expressed in terminal site of malignant cell differentiation.
source: Transcription factor (TF) TWIST1 was highly expressed in terminal site.
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis of malignant cells.

claim: The highly expressed DEGs in cluster 1 of malignant cells were related to behaviors such as ECM organization, response to transforming growth factor (TGF) β, regulation of epithelial cell proliferation and migration.
source: We observed that the highly expressed DEGs in cluster 1 were related to behaviors such as ECM organization, response to transforming growth factor (TGF) β, regulation of epithelial cell proliferation and migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of DEGs shown in the referenced figure.

claim: TF TWIST1 and its corresponding coexpression module in the subcluster 1 had higher area under curve (AUC) scores and expression levels.
source: Among them, TF TWIST1 and its corresponding coexpression module in the subcluster 1 had higher area under curve (AUC) scores and expression levels (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on SCENIC analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Genes in TWIST1 target coexpression module contained a variety of collagen-encoding genes such as MMP2.
source: We observed that genes in TWIST1 target coexpression module contained a variety of collagen-encoding genes such as MMP2, indicate that TWIST1 may affect the structures of the ECM by regulating matrix metalloproteinase 2 (MMP2).
evidence: This is based on SCENIC coexpression module analysis.

claim: The genes in the TWIST1 coexpression module may be involved in biological processes related to tumor degeneration, such as epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and response to TGF-β.
source: Further GO functional enrichment disclosed that the genes in the TWIST1 coexpression module may be involved in biological processes related to tumor degeneration, such as epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and response to TGF-β (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: After the transfection of cells with TWIST1, EMT pathway proteins were activated, and the invasion and migration abilities of melanoma A375 cells were enhanced.
source: The assays confirmed that after the transfection of cells with TWIST1, EMT pathway proteins were activated, and the invasion and migration abilities of melanoma A375 cells were enhanced.
evidence: This is based on western blot, wound-healing and Transwell assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: TWIST1 is one of the EMT-inducer prototypes.
source: TWIST1 is one of the EMT-inducer prototypes (Li et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: The subcluster with high activity of TWIST1 had stronger interaction strength with stroma cells.
source: Therefore, we analyzed the interactions between different malignant cell subclusters and other cell types, and showed that the subcluster with high activity of TWIST1 had stronger interaction strength with stroma cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on cell-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Cells in subcluster 1 interact with receptors of stromal cells such as fibroblasts, through COL1A1-ITGA2 and other collagen pathways.
source: Cells in subcluster 1 interact with receptors of stromal cells such as fibroblasts, through COL1A1-ITGA2 and other collagen pathways (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Integrin α2 (ITGA2) triggers cancer cell adhesion to collagen, promotes cell migration, anoikis resistance, mesothelial clearance, and peritoneal metastasis.
source: Integrin α2 (ITGA2) triggers cancer cell adhesion to collagen, promotes cell migration, anoikis resistance, mesothelial clearance, and peritoneal metastasis (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2020.

claim: TF TWIST1 in malignant cells may promote the secretion of collagen signals and interact with integrin proteins generated by fibroblasts to destroy the integrity of e-cadherin; thus, driving the EMT and metastasis.
source: These results suggest that TF TWIST1 in malignant cells may promote the secretion of collagen signals and interact with integrin proteins generated by fibroblasts to destroy the integrity of e-cadherin; thus, driving the EMT and metastasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed interactions and known functions of the molecules.

claim: A reclustering analysis of macrophages distinguished macrophages into two cell types, M1 (HLA-DQA2+) and M2 (CD163+).
source: A reclustering analysis of macrophages distinguished macrophages into two cell types, M1 (HLA-DQA2+) and M2 (CD163+), among which the tumor-infiltrating macrophages were primarily of the M2 type (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on reclustering and marker gene analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The tumor-infiltrating macrophages were primarily of the M2 type.
source: A reclustering analysis of macrophages distinguished macrophages into two cell types, M1 (HLA-DQA2+) and M2 (CD163+), among which the tumor-infiltrating macrophages were primarily of the M2 type (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on cell type composition analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The activities of the three motifs, IRF4, KLF9, and SOX18, were downregulated, and the activation of STAT1, REL, and NF-κB1 motifs resulted in M2 polarization process.
source: Combined with the key motifs identified by SCENIC, we observed that the activities of the three motifs, IRF4, KLF9, and SOX18, were downregulated, and the activation of STAT1, REL, and NF-κB1 motifs resulted in this M2 polarization process (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on SCENIC analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: There was a strong cell interaction between M2 cells and malignant cells.
source: The cell communication weight demonstrated that there was a strong cell interaction between M2 cells and malignant cells, and there was also a certain cell interaction with M1 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on CellChat analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M1 cells primarily secreted tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, whereas M2 cells secreted TGF-β.
source: Among them, M1 cells primarily secreted tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, whereas M2 cells secreted TGF-β (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: M2 cells affected M1 macrophages through the galectin signaling pathway.
source: Furthermore, M2 cells affected M1 macrophages through the galectin signaling pathway (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on signaling pathway analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: EREG was highly expressed in M2 cells.
source: The heatmap of pseudotime gene dynamic expression inferred from splicing kinetics suggested that EREG was highly expressed in M2 cells (Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Patients with melanoma with high expression of EREG in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort had a lower survival rate.
source: Moreover, patients with melanoma with high expression of EREG in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort had a lower survival rate (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis using TCGA data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: M2 cells with high expression of EREG also expressed CD44.
source: We divided the M2-type macrophages into two groups of high and low of EREG expression, and the differential analyses revealed that M2 cells with high expression of EREG also expressed CD44 (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The MIF ligand molecules affected M1 and M2 macrophages through the CD44 receptor.
source: The MIF ligand molecules affected M1 and M2 macrophages through the CD44 receptor.
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis.

claim: MIF is a macrophage migration inhibitory molecule.
source: MIF is a macrophage migration inhibitory molecule (Donn and Ray, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Donn and Ray, 2004.

claim: The migration ability of M2 cells with a high expression of EREG decreases.
source: MIF is a macrophage migration inhibitory molecule (Donn and Ray, 2004), which implies that the migration ability of M2 cells with a high expression of EREG decreases.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of MIF and the expression of CD44 in EREG-high M2 cells.

claim: M2 cells with a low expression of EREG were enriched in the pathway related to macrophage migration.
source: Simultaneously, M2 cells with a low expression of EREG were enriched in the pathway related to macrophage migration (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: B-cell subclusters were divided into naive B (IGHM+), memory B (CD27+), germinal center B (BCL6+), and plasma cells (CD38+).
source: We divided the B-cell subclusters into naive B (IGHM+), memory B (CD27+), germinal center B (BCL6+), and plasma cells (CD38+) (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression and cell type annotation shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The germinal center B cells and plasma cells were detected at the beginning and end of the pseudotime, respectively.
source: The germinal center B cells and plasma cells were detected at the beginning and end of the pseudotime, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The germinal center B cells acted on the CD44 receptors of malignant cells through the LGALS9 ligand.
source: The germinal center B cells acted on the CD44 receptors of malignant cells through the LGALS9 ligand, whereas the malignant cells acted on the CD74+ CXCR4 and CD74+ CD44 receptors of various types of B cells primarily through the MIF ligand molecules.
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The malignant cells acted on the CD74+ CXCR4 and CD74+ CD44 receptors of various types of B cells primarily through the MIF ligand molecules.
source: The germinal center B cells acted on the CD44 receptors of malignant cells through the LGALS9 ligand, whereas the malignant cells acted on the CD74+ CXCR4 and CD74+ CD44 receptors of various types of B cells primarily through the MIF ligand molecules.
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The MIF/CD74 signaling pathway plays a vital role in maintaining the survival of germinal center B cells and enhancing the antigen presentation of B cells.
source: It has been reported that the MIF/CD74 signaling pathway plays a vital role in maintaining the survival of germinal center B cells and enhancing the antigen presentation of B cells (Lantner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lantner et al., 2007.

claim: B-cell infiltration primarily inhibited cancer cells in AM.
source: The above-described results suggested that B-cell infiltration primarily inhibited cancer cells in AM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed B cell-malignant cell interactions.

claim: T cells were annotated into nine subclusters, including CD4+ T cells (CD4_NaiveLike, Th1, Tfh, and Treg) and CD8+ T cells (CD8_NaiveLike, CD8_EarlyActiv, CD8_EffectorMemory, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex).
source: ProjecTILs was used to annotate T cells in the data into nine subclusters, including CD4+ T cells (CD4_NaiveLike, Th1, Tfh, and Treg) and CD8+ T cells (CD8_NaiveLike, CD8_EarlyActiv, CD8_EffectorMemory, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on ProjecTILs annotation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CD4+ T cells were gradually differentiated into Tregs, which corresponded to the characteristic gene set (cluster 3), represented by FOXP3.
source: CD4+ T cells were gradually differentiated into Tregs, which corresponded to the characteristic gene set (cluster 3), represented by FOXP3 (Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: FOXP3 is a key regulator of regulatory T (Treg) cell gene expression, which can activate the expression of TNFRSF18, IL2RA, and CTLA4 and inhibit the expression of IL2 and IFNG in association with TF RUNX1.
source: FOXP3 is a key regulator of regulatory T (Treg) cell gene expression, which can activate the expression of TNFRSF18, IL2RA, and CTLA4 and inhibit the expression of IL2 and IFNG in association with TF RUNX1 (Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2006.

claim: CD8+ T cells gradually transformed from CD8_NaiveLike to exhausted (or pre-exhausted) T cells (CD8_Tpex, CD8_Tex) along the pseudotime trajectory.
source: The pseudotime trajectory depicted the difference in the gene expression of CD8+ T cells from CD8_NaiveLike to exhausted (or pre-exhausted) T cells (CD8_Tpex, CD8_Tex) (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In the CD8+ T pseudotime gene clustering heatmap, with the direction of pseudotime, the CD8+ T cells gradually transformed from cluster 3 genes with the high expression of GNLY and IGHG1 to cluster 2 genes with the high expression of GZMK and IFNG.
source: In the CD8+ T pseudotime gene clustering heatmap, with the direction of pseudotime, the CD8+ T cells gradually transformed from cluster 3 genes with the high expression of GNLY and IGHG1 to cluster 2 genes with the high expression of GZMK and IFNG.
evidence: This is based on pseudotime gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: In terminal cluster 1 of CD8+ T cells, the exhausted genes represented by LAG3, were highly expressed.
source: In terminal cluster 1, the exhausted genes represented by LAG3, were highly expressed (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is based on pseudotime gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Treg, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex interact strongly with malignant cells.
source: Treg, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex interact strongly with malignant cells.
evidence: This is based on cell-cell interaction analysis.

claim: Malignant cells use MIF and MDK as their major ligands to produce molecular links with various T-cell receptors.
source: Mechanistically, malignant cells use MIF and MDK as their major ligands to produce molecular links with various T-cell receptors, which may play an important role in regulating the exhaustion of T cells in the TMEs.
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis.

claim: Compared with the well-known immune checkpoints PDCD1 and CTLA-4, the expression of TNFRSF9 in exhausted T cells is higher in AM.
source: Moreover, compared with the well-known immune checkpoints PDCD1 and CTLA-4, the expression of TNFRSF9 in exhausted T cells is higher.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis in AM T cells.

claim: In CM T-cell data, the expression of PDCD1 and CTLA-4 was higher than that of TNFRSF9.
source: Conversely, the CM T-cell data obtained from a previously published melanoma single-cell dataset that we downloaded, the expression of PDCD1 and CTLA-4 was higher than that of TNFRSF9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis in CM T cells shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Malignant cells will be more specific to Tregs, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex through the TNFRSF9 receptor expressed by the TNFSF9 ligand.
source: Simultaneously, malignant cells will be more specific to Tregs, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex through the TNFRSF9 receptor expressed by the TNFSF9 ligand, which suggests that TNFRSF9 may be a more suitable immune check target for the treatment of AM (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: TNFRSF9 may be a more suitable immune check target for the treatment of AM.
source: Simultaneously, malignant cells will be more specific to Tregs, CD8_Tpex, and CD8_Tex through the TNFRSF9 receptor expressed by the TNFSF9 ligand, which suggests that TNFRSF9 may be a more suitable immune check target for the treatment of AM (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed expression patterns and interactions.

claim: CAFs were divided into three subclusters: iCAF (RGS4+), mCAF (PDGFRA+), and a new CAF cluster that highly expressed CTGF.
source: Therefore, we then divided CAFs into three subclusters. Along with the traditional iCAF (RGS4+) and mCAF (PDGFRA+) cell clusters, we detected a new CAF cluster that highly expressed CTGF (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on reclustering and marker gene analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The iCAF cluster was associated with the BMP signaling pathway, ECM organization, and extracellular structure organization.
source: The iCAF cluster was associated with the BMP signaling pathway, ECM organization, and extracellular structure organization.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mCAF cluster was associated with the functions of muscle cells and tissues.
source: The mCAF cluster was associated with the functions of muscle cells and tissues.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The CTGF+ CAF cluster was associated with functions such as cell growth, response to hypoxia, and protein folding.
source: The CTGF+ CAF cluster was associated with functions such as cell growth, response to hypoxia, and protein folding.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The TWIST1 motif was highly activated in iCAFs.
source: The SCENIC results revealed that the TWIST1 motif was highly activated in iCAFs, and the TBX2 motif was highly activated in mCAFs.
evidence: This is based on SCENIC analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The TBX2 motif was highly activated in mCAFs.
source: The SCENIC results revealed that the TWIST1 motif was highly activated in iCAFs, and the TBX2 motif was highly activated in mCAFs.
evidence: This is based on SCENIC analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CTGF+ CAFs activate the NFATC4 and SOX10 motifs.
source: Specifically, CTGF+ CAFs activate the NFATC4 and SOX10 motifs (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is based on SCENIC analysis shown in Figures 6C and 6D.

claim: NFATC4 was the upstream TF of CTGF.
source: In addition, the results of SCENIC inferred that NFATC4 was the upstream TF of CTGF and NFATC4 target genes were enriched in GO terms, such as mesenchymal cell proliferation and ECM organization.
evidence: This is based on SCENIC analysis.

claim: NFATC4 target genes were enriched in GO terms, such as mesenchymal cell proliferation and ECM organization.
source: In addition, the results of SCENIC inferred that NFATC4 was the upstream TF of CTGF and NFATC4 target genes were enriched in GO terms, such as mesenchymal cell proliferation and ECM organization.
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis of NFATC4 target genes.

claim: The patient cluster with a high expression of NFATC4 target genes had a lower survival rate.
source: The melanoma patient cohort in TCGA was divided into two clusters according to the NFATC4 target genes expression patterns, and the patient cluster with a high expression of NFATC4 target genes had a lower survival rate (Figure 6E, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on survival analysis using TCGA data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Compared to the PLs, the expression of CTGF+ CAFs in the LG increases.
source: Compared to the PLs, the expression of CTGF+ CAFs in the LG increases, which suggests that the secreted protein CTGF plays a vital regulatory role in the metastasis of malignant cells (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is based on cell type composition analysis shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: The secreted protein CTGF plays a vital regulatory role in the metastasis of malignant cells.
source: Compared to the PLs, the expression of CTGF+ CAFs in the LG increases, which suggests that the secreted protein CTGF plays a vital regulatory role in the metastasis of malignant cells (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased expression of CTGF+ CAFs in metastatic tissue.

claim: CTGF significantly increased the colony formation and cell migration ability of A375 cells.
source: By adding 50 ng/ml CTGF during the A375 culture process, we observed that CTGF significantly increased the colony formation and cell migration ability of A375 cells (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This is based on colony formation and Transwell assays shown in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: CTGF+ CAFs may further impact tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) by the M2-type macrophages through ligand-receptor molecules, such as SPP1-CD44, PTN-NCL, and MDK-NCL.
source: Moreover, CTGF+ CAFs may further impact tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) by the M2-type macrophages through ligand-receptor molecules, such as SPP1-CD44, PTN-NCL, and MDK-NCL (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on ligand-receptor interaction analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The M1-type macrophages can inhibit and phagocytose tumor cells, whereas the M2-type macrophages play immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting roles.
source: The M1-type macrophages can inhibit and phagocytose tumor cells, whereas the M2-type macrophages play immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting roles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about macrophage subtypes.

claim: The M2-type macrophages with a high expression of EREG had a weaker migration ability, but their ability to promote tumor development is stronger.
source: We observed that the M2-type macrophages with a high expression of EREG had a weaker migration ability, but their ability to promote tumor development is stronger; thus, creating an immunosuppressive microenvironment.
evidence: This is based on the differential analysis and pathway enrichment of EREG-high vs EREG-low M2 cells.

claim: Antibodies that can block cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) and programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) have been marketed and have achieved remarkable results in the treatment of melanoma.
source: Considering the elimination of immunosuppressive CD8+ T cells in the TME as an example (Topalian et al., 2016), antibodies that can block cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) and programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) have been marketed and have achieved remarkable results in the treatment of melanoma (Eroglu et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Topalian et al., 2016 and Eroglu et al., 2015.

claim: Although these drugs have improved survival in patients with advanced-stage disease, their efficacy is limited, and the response rate is low for AM, which is more common in the Asian population.
source: Nevertheless, although these drugs have improved survival in patients with advanced-stage disease, their efficacy is limited, and the response rate is low for AM, which is more common in the Asian population.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of current immunotherapy for AM.

claim: TNFRSF9 was highly expressed in CD8+ T cells in the AM microenvironment, and existed at the end of the pseudotime trajectory, while PDCD1 and CTLA4 expression levels were relatively low.
source: At the transcriptional level, our data found that TNFRSF9 was highly expressed in CD8+ T cells in the AM microenvironment, and existed at the end of the pseudotime trajectory, while PDCD1 and CTLA4 expression levels were relatively low.
evidence: This is based on gene expression and pseudotime analysis of CD8+ T cells.

claim: TNFRSF9 is an important activated immune checkpoint molecule on surface of T cells.
